text: Large trees are keystone structures in many terrestrial ecosystems. They contribute disproportionately to reproduction, recruitment and succession, and influence the structure, dynamics and diversity of forests. Recently, researchers have become concerned about evidence showing rapid declines in large, old trees in a range of ecosystems across the globe. We used ≥10 cm diameter at breast height (DBH) stem inventory data from 20, 0.5 ha forest plots spanning the wet tropical rainforest of Queensland, Australia to examine the contribution of large-diameter trees to above ground biomass (AGB), richness, dominance, mortality and recruitment. We show consistencies with tropical rainforest globally in that large-diameter trees (≥70 cm DBH) contribute much of the biomass (33%) from few trees (2.4% of stems ≥10 cm DBH) with the density of the largest trees explaining much of the variation (62%) in AGB across plots. text: Dense populations of large trees—defined as those with a diameter at breast height (DBH) of 10 centimeters or more—play a dominant role in structuring terrestrial forest biomass and diversity. Across 20, 0.5-hectare plots in the wet tropical rainforests of Queensland, Australia, large-diameter trees (those 70 cm or greater in DBH) accounted for roughly one-third of total above-ground biomass, while comprising only about 2.4% of all stems measured. Notably, the biomass of the top 5% of trees is sufficient to predict total plot biomass with about 85% accuracy. This pattern, driven by the high density of both large and moderately sized trees, fosters substantial resilience to disturbances and potential impacts from global environmental change. Overall, the persistence of these large trees and the high species richness in this ecosystem promote the maintenance of substantial above-ground biomass into the future.

text:
Large trees are keystone structures within many terrestrial ecosystems, significantly influencing reproduction, recruitment, and succession, as well as the structure, dynamics, and diversity of forests. Recent research has highlighted concerns over rapid declines in the largest, oldest trees globally. Here, using inventory data from 20 plots, each 0.5 ha in size, in the wet tropical rainforest of Queensland, Australia (with trees ≥10 cm diameter at breast height), we analyzed the roles of large-diameter trees in above-ground biomass (AGB), species richness, dominance, mortality, and recruitment.

Our results align with global trends in tropical rainforests, where trees ≥70 cm in DBH account for about one-third of above-ground biomass, even though they represent only about 2.4% of all stems measured (≥10 cm DBH). Plot-specific AGB is largely determined by the density of the largest trees, which explain 62% of the variation in AGB across the study sites. Notably, estimating AGB from the largest 5% of trees yields predictions with around 85% accuracy.

In contrast to rainforests in Africa and the Americas, Australian wet tropical rainforests exhibit greater species capacity to reach large diameters, resulting in relatively modest biomass hyperdominance—only about 10% of species produce 50% of the biomass. This pattern suggests higher potential resilience to local disturbances and to global environmental pressures.

Our findings indicate that the high biomass of Australian wet tropical rainforests is primarily due to the abundant presence of large and medium-sized trees. These conditions suggest that such forests may maintain their current biomass levels and large-tree densities under future environmental pressures, supported by a rich diversity of large tree species and numerous smaller replacements.

text:
Blood cultures are considered the gold standard to distinguish bacteremia from non-bacteremic systemic inflammation. In current clinical practice, bacteraemia is considered unlikely if blood cultures have been negative for 48–72 hours. Modern BC systems have reduced this time-to-positivity (TTP), questioning whether the time frame of 48–72 hrs is still valid. This study investigates the distribution of TTP, the probability of blood culture positivity after 24 hours, and identifies clinical predictors of prolonged TTP.

Adult patients with monomicrobial bacteremia in an academic hospital were included retrospectively over a three-year period. Clinical data were retrieved from the medical records. Predictors of TTP >24 hours were determined by uni- and multivariate analyses. The residual probability of bacteremia was estimated for the scenario of negative BCs at 24 hours after bedside collection.

The cohort consisted of 801 patients, accounting for 897 episodes of bacteremia. Mean age was 65 years (IQR 54–73), 534 (59.5%) patients were male. Median TTP was 15.7 (IQR 13.5–19.3) hours. TTP was ≤24 hours in 85.3% of episodes. Antibiotic pre-treatment (adjusted OR 1.77; 95%CI 1.14–2.74, p<0.01) was independently associated with prolonged TTP. The probability of bacteremia, if BC had remained negative for 24 hours, was 1.8% (95% CI 1.46–2.14).

With adequate hospital logistics, the probability of positive blood cultures after 24 hours of negative cultures was low. Combined with clinical reassessment, knowledge of this low probability may contribute to prioritization of the differential diagnosis and decisions on antimicrobial therapy. As a potential antibiotic stewardship tool, this strategy warrants further prospective investigation.

An area of high concern is how this situation affects vulnerable families and their children. A key pathway in improving the situation for children in times of conflict is to reinforce maternal agency, for instance, through education. However, the state of the art of research lacks a clear understanding of how many years of education is needed before children benefit. Due to mother’s differing social context and ability, the effect of maternal education varies. We study the heterogeneous treatment effects of maternal agency, here operationalized as length of education, on severe child undernutrition in the context of armed conflict. We deploy a repeated cross-sectional study design, using the Nigeria 2008 and 2013 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS). The sample covers 25,917 children and their respective mothers. A key methodological challenge is to estimate this heterogeneity inductively. The causal inference literature proposes a machine learning approach, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART), as a promising avenue to overcome this challenge. Based on BART-estimation of the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) this study confirms earlier findings in that maternal education decreases severe child undernutrition, but only when mothers acquire an education that lasts more than the country’s compulsory 9 years; that is 10 years of education and higher. This protective effect remains even during the exposure of armed conflict.

text:
A rapidly developing yet conflict-affected African economy such as Nigeria faces persistent challenges, including armed conflict, poverty, and high rates of child morbidity. Notably, the welfare of vulnerable families, especially children, is significantly shaped by the level of maternal education—a form of maternal agency. However, the literature has not yet established a precise threshold regarding the minimum duration of maternal schooling required to produce measurable reductions in severe child undernutrition, particularly within conflict zones. Prior research underscores heterogeneity in maternal social contexts and capacities, implying that the impact of maternal education is not uniform across all households.

This study employs a repeated cross-sectional survey design, analyzing data from the 2008 and 2013 Nigerian Demographic and Health Surveys, encompassing 25,917 children and their mothers. To address the complexity of heterogeneity in maternal education effects, the researchers utilize Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) to estimate Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATEs). The results indicate that increased maternal education—specifically, attainment beyond the compulsory school level of nine years—confers protection against severe child undernutrition. Maternal education of at least ten years or more is associated with reduced risk of severe undernutrition among children, even under conditions of ongoing armed conflict. These findings highlight the importance of targeting maternal education as a strategic intervention to improve child health outcomes in conflict-affected settings.

text:
Nigeria, a rapidly growing African economy, continues to grapple with armed conflict, poverty, and high rates of child morbidity. Of particular concern is the impact of these conditions on vulnerable families and their children. One promising strategy to enhance child outcomes during conflict is to strengthen maternal agency—particularly through education. However, the scientific literature remains unclear about the minimum required years of maternal education necessary to achieve benefits for children.

This study examines the heterogeneous effects of maternal education—measured as years of schooling—on severe child undernutrition during periods of armed conflict in Nigeria. Using repeated cross-sectional data from the 2008 and 2013 Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), which encompass a sample of 25,917 children and their mothers, we assess these impacts. A central challenge is quantifying the heterogeneity in maternal effects, addressed here via Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART), a machine learning method for estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATEs).

Our results confirm prior findings: maternal education reduces severe child undernutrition only when mothers complete at least 10 years of schooling or more—the threshold above Nigeria’s compulsory education level—regardless of the presence of conflict. This protective effect persists even in conflict-affected settings.

text:
This two-step study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) for presurgery staging of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in France (EVIEPEB; ClinicalTrial.gov identifier NCT00960271).

Step 1 consisted of a high-benchmark EBUS-TBNA–training program in participating hospital centers. Step 2 was a prospective, national, multicenter study on patients with confirmed or suspected NSCLC and an indication for mediastinal staging with at least one lymph node > 1 cm in diameter. Patients with negative or uninformative EBUS-TBNA and positron-emission tomography-positive or -negative nodes, respectively, underwent either mediastinoscopy or surgery. Direct costs related to final diagnosis of node status were prospectively recorded.

Sixteen of 22 participating centers were certified by the EBUS-TBNA–training program and enrolled 163 patients in Step 2. EBUS-TBNA was informative for 149 (91%) patients (75 malignant, 74 non-malignant) and uninformative for 14 (9%). Mediastinoscopy was avoided for 80% of the patients. With a 52% malignant-node rate, EBUS-TBNA positive- and negative-predictive values, respectively, were 100% and 90%. EBUS-TBNA was cost-effective, with expected savings of €1,450 per patient, and would have remained cost-effective even if all EBUS-TBNAs had been performed under general anesthesia or the cost of the procedure had been 30% higher (expected cost-saving of €994 and €1,427 per patient, respectively).

After EBUS-TBNA training and certification of participating centers, the results of this prospective multicenter study confirmed EBUS-TBNA cost-effectiveness for NSCLC staging.

text:
A two-step trial assessed the cost-effectiveness of endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) for mediastinal staging in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in France. In the first step, a standardized EBUS-TBNA training was conducted at selected hospitals. The second, multicenter, prospective study enrolled patients with likely NSCLC and at least one target lymph node larger than 1 cm. EBUS-TBNA was performed; when results were negative or inconclusive, patients proceeded with either mediastinoscopy or surgery based on PET scan findings. Costs for the procedures directly related to node status determination were recorded.

Of 163 patients enrolled, EBUS-TBNA provided an informative result in 91% (149 patients), yielding a node positivity rate of 52%. The test demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy—with perfect positive and strong positive predictive values (100% and 90%, respectively). The intervention avoided mediastinoscopy in 80% of cases. Economic analysis showed that EBUS-TBNA was cost-effective, generating an average saving of €1,450 per patient. Even if EBUS-TBNA had been performed under general anesthesia or its cost increased by 30%, cost savings remained substantial (€994 and €1,427 per patient, respectively). Overall, the study confirmed that EBUS-TBNA is cost-effective for NSCLC staging after proper training and center certification.

text:
More than 50 years after the end of the Korean War, recently released documents provide more detail on the mass murder of around 100,000 South Koreans by their own government in the war's first weeks.

According to the Associated Press, South Korean investigators have gained access to newly declassified records that show that the American military did nothing to intervene. The mass executions of between 100,000 and 300,000 leftists and others during these purges in 1950 are said to have been carried out to stop them from joining the attacking North Korean Forces.

The Associated Press says that the documents show no evidence that General Douglas MacArthur took action to halt or slow the summary executions, despite having knowledge of them.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission was commissioned by South Korea in 2005 to, amongst other things, uncover the truth of what happened during those first few weeks of the war. Evidence of the executions was suppressed during the authoritarian presidency of Park Chung-hee.

According to Workers World Party, Ahn Byung-ook, president of the commission, has identified 215 cases where United States forces were directly involved, out of a total of over 1,400 incidents of mass murder.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which has a mandate to continue work through 2010, still has tens of thousands of declassified documents to read through.

text: After the Korean War ended in 1953, new documents have emerged, offering greater detail about the mass killings carried out by South Korean authorities in the war’s early days. Recent investigations by South Korean officials have gained access to declassified records that describe how roughly 100,000 to 300,000 people, including leftists and others, were executed on orders to prevent their enlistment with the North Korean military. These purges took place in the first weeks of 1950. text:
All residents within a half-mile radius of the EQ Resource Recovery chemical plant in southeastern Michigan were asked to voluntarily evacuate on Tuesday due to a chemical plant explosion. ClickOnDetroit reported that nearby residents who choose to stay were told to close their doors and windows.

The plant, located in Romulus, near Wayne, is about 15 miles southwest of Detroit. Initial reports stated that a single explosion in a chemical tank was the cause of the fire. The cause of this explosion has not yet been determined. Detroit ABC affiliate WXYZ confirmed that all employees made it out of the plant before the explosion occurred, and that HAZMAT teams were on the scene of the fire. Wayne County Sheriff Warren Evans announced that no injuries were reported in the initial explosion. However, approximately 32 people were treated for breathing problems at nearby Oakwood Annapolis Hospital, due to the subsequent fire.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) analyzed soot in the area and determined that it did not pose a substantial health risk. The company in question has been the target of numerous enforcement actions by the EPA in the past, including a $240,000 fine in 1999. A major chemical processed at the plant is acetone, the main ingredient in nail polish remover, which is known to be toxic in high dosages, especially to those with lung conditions. Acetone is also an eye and skin irritant. Other chemicals, such as antifreeze, are also processed there. Two Detroit-area law firms have filed class action lawsuits against EQ Resource Recovery on behalf of local residents, and a third is considering similar action.

Romulus is the site of the Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), the primary airport for the Detroit area and a hub for Northwest Airlines. However, airport service was not affected. News of this explosion came as a chemical plant explosion in Story City, Iowa happened just a day before and three similar explosions in Texas occurred July 28.

text:
Copenhagen – The Danish people have voted to keep the current centre-right political coalition of the Venstre (The Liberal Party), Det Konservative Folkeparti (Conservative People's Party) and the Dansk Folkeparti (Danish People's Party).

Prime Minister Anders Fogh Rasmussen's Liberal Party retained the largest number of seats in parliament. The governing coalition between the Liberals and Conservative People's Party remained intact. They will likely be supported largely by the Danish People's Party, which gained 2 seats. The Radikale Venstre (Radical Left) party gained the most seats of any party, although it remains outside the governing group of parties. The election marked the second time in a row that the Social Democrats were not the largest party in the parliament, a change from most of the 20th century. The party lost 5 seats and leader Mogens Lykketoft resigned immediately after the election.

The largest opposition party, the Socialdemokraterne (Social Democrats) led by Mogens Lykketoft focused on employment, which they claim has decreased under the current government.

text:
Wikinews has learned through an investigation that anonymous edits on the Wikipedia article Chris Benoit were added about the death of his wife Nancy Benoit 14 hours before police entered the Benoit home to find the former professional World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) Canadian wrestler and his family dead.

Further investigation shows that the IP address used to make the first edit is located in Connecticut, but the IP address is not linked to any computers or servers used by the WWE, but according to Cary Bass, Volunteer Coordinator for the Wikimedia Foundation, the IP address matches a location in Stamford, Connecticut where the WWE headquarters is located. Bass also informed the local authorities in Atlanta about the unusual edits, but it is not known if the edits were investigated by the police. The second edit was made by a computer in Australia from a wireless network.

Earlier, on Saturday afternoon, Chris Benoit placed a series of calls that explained why he missed his flight to Houston. The stories he told were mostly about his wife and son being sick with food poisoning and vomiting. Although, in one call he said that he and Nancy were at the hospital to be with Daniel who was hospitalized. Throughout he insisted that he would attend that live event in Houston.

When he missed the live event on Sunday, and the WWE couldn't get hold of him, they contacted authorities. Police say that Benoit strangled his wife on Friday, smothered his son on late Friday or early Saturday, and then hanged himself inside his weight room on Sunday or Monday.

The Wikinews investigation is unable to conclude whether the anonymous editors had inside information about the death of Nancy Benoit.

This is not the first time Benoit's article has been edited to show false or unsourced information, as the article's edit history indicates a long history of promotional spam and vandalism. Around the time of the edits, the article contained a hidden warning to editors of the section mentioned, warning against adding rumours and speculations. For the time being, Benoit's article has been protected in an attempt to stop the addition of fraudulent information.

text:
Authorities in the United States are reviewing recent changes made to the Wikipedia page on Canadian professional wrestler Chris Benoit. According to a Wikinews investigation, anonymous edits were posted to the article fourteen hours before police entered the Benoit residence and discovered the bodies of Benoit, his wife Nancy, and their son Daniel. These modifications came after Benoit had called emergency services for himself and his family earlier that weekend, explaining in the calls that Nancy and Daniel were suffering from severe food poisoning. He insisted he would still attend a WWE live event in Houston.

Investigations by Wikinews determined that the first of these anonymous edits originated from an internet protocol (IP) address located in Stamford, Connecticut—a city where WWE’s headquarters are situated. A representative from the Wikimedia Foundation confirmed this, indicating the IP is linked to the area around WWE’s central office. However, the IP address does not correspond to any personal computer or server used by WWE staff. A second anonymous edit traced back to a network in Australia was also made in the same timeframe.

Police reports indicate that Benoit reportedly killed his wife and son sometime between Friday and Sunday before taking his own life. WWE was unable to reach Benoit and prompted law enforcement intervention. At this point, it is unclear whether the recent Wikipedia edits were made by individuals with any prior knowledge of the tragedy, though such a possibility cannot be ruled out based on the available evidence.

The Benoit article has a long history of being targeted by unreliable or misleading edits and has previously been protected to prevent the spread of unverified information and vandalism. Editing access to the page has been temporarily restricted pending further investigation into the authenticity of the recent changes.

When he missed the live event on Sunday, and the WWE couldn't get hold of him, they contacted authorities. Police say that Benoit strangled his wife on Friday, smothered his son on late Friday or early Saturday, and then hanged himself inside his weight room on Sunday or Monday.

The Wikinews investigation is unable to conclude whether the anonymous editors had inside information about the death of Nancy Benoit.

text:
HIV/AIDS activist Phyu Phyu Thin has been released from police custody in Myanmar, after being detained more than a month ago.

A supporter of the National League for Democracy (NLD), Phyu Phyu Thin heads the NLD's volunteer HIV/AIDS relief effort, in which she visits patients' boarding houses and homes and helps them obtain free treatment from international organizations, such as Médecins Sans Frontières.

She has been an outspoken critic of the Burmese military government's handling of HIV/AIDS, saying not enough is being done.

Phyu Phyu Thin was taken from her home by police on May 21, after she had participated in a march calling for the release of Aung San Suu Kyi, the detained leader of the NLD.

She was never charged with a crime, she said. She was released at around 9 p.m. local time last night (0230 GMT) from a detention center in Yangon.

While in detention, Phyu Phyu Thin engaged in a hunger strike, taking only liquids for about a week, which left her very weak.

The United States Department of State had issued a statement last week, calling on the Myanmar junta to release Phyu Phyu Thin.

While Phyu Phyu Thin was being held, 11 HIV/AIDS patients were detained last month for a few days at a hospital after they had held demonstrations, calling for her release.

Phyu Phyu Thin's release follows the release of 51 NLD supporters who also were detained last month in a government crackdown on the NLD's prayer vigils for Suu Kyi.

Phyu Phyu Thin, 36, had previously been detained in 2000, after she and other supporters were bundled away by special police from a rally for Suu Kyi. She and the others were held in Insein prison.

The U.S. military largely avoided direct combat with Iraqi forces and experienced very few casualties. Most information about Iraqi losses remained hidden. This left the public unable to tell how much of what they witnessed was authentic and how much was staged.

text:
Dynamic programming is both a mathematical optimization method and a computer programming method. The method was developed by Richard Bellman in the 1950s and has found applications in numerous fields, from aerospace engineering to economics.
In both contexts it refers to simplifying a complicated problem by breaking it down into simpler sub-problems in a recursive manner. While some decision problems cannot be taken apart this way, decisions that span several points in time do often break apart recursively. Likewise, in computer science, if a problem can be solved optimally by breaking it into sub-problems and then recursively finding the optimal solutions to the sub-problems, then it is said to have optimal substructure.
If sub-problems can be nested recursively inside larger problems, so that dynamic programming methods are applicable, then there is a relation between the value of the larger problem and the values of the sub-problems. In the optimization literature this relationship is called the Bellman equation.

text: Dynamic programming is a mathematical optimization technique and a computer programming approach developed by Richard Bellman in the 1950s, with applications spanning aerospace engineering, economics, and other disciplines. It operates by decomposing a complex problem into simpler, overlapping sub-problems, which are solved recursively. This method is particularly effective for decision problems that unfold over time, where choices at one stage influence future stages. A problem is suitable for dynamic programming if it exhibits optimal substructure—meaning an optimal solution to the overall problem can be constructed from optimal solutions to its sub-problems. When sub-problems are nested within larger ones, a recursive relationship emerges between the value of the larger problem and the values of its components. In optimization theory, this recursive relationship is formally known as the Bellman equation, which provides a foundational framework for solving sequential decision problems efficiently. Not all problems admit such decomposition, but those that do benefit from structured, recursive solution strategies grounded in this principle.

Dynamic programming is both a mathematical optimization method and a computer programming method. The method was developed by Richard Bellman in the 1950s and has found applications in numerous fields, from aerospace engineering to economics.
In both contexts it refers to simplifying a complicated problem by breaking it down into simpler sub-problems in a recursive manner. While some decision problems cannot be taken apart this way, decisions that span several points in time do often break apart recursively. Likewise, in computer science, if a problem can be solved optimally by breaking it into sub-problems and then recursively finding the optimal solutions to the sub-problems, then it is said to have optimal substructure.
If sub-problems can be nested recursively inside larger problems, so that dynamic programming methods are applicable, then there is a relation between the value of the larger problem and the values of the sub-problems. In the optimization literature this relationship is called the Bellman equation.
</source>

text:
Hyperspectral imaging collects and processes information from across the electromagnetic spectrum. The goal of hyperspectral imaging is to obtain the spectrum for each pixel in the image of a scene, with the purpose of finding objects, identifying materials, or detecting processes. There are three general branches of spectral imagers. There are push broom scanners and the related whisk broom scanners (spatial scanning), which read images over time, band sequential scanners (spectral scanning), which acquire images of an area at different wavelengths, and snapshot hyperspectral imaging, which uses a staring array to generate an image in an instant.
Whereas the human eye sees color of visible light in mostly three bands (long wavelengths - perceived as red, medium wavelengths - perceived as green, and short wavelengths - perceived as blue), spectral imaging divides the spectrum into many more bands. This technique of dividing images into bands can be extended beyond the visible. In hyperspectral imaging, the recorded spectra have fine wavelength resolution and cover a wide range of wavelengths. Hyperspectral imaging measures continuous spectral bands, as opposed to multiband imaging which measures spaced spectral bands.
Engineers build hyperspectral sensors and processing systems for applications in astronomy, agriculture, molecular biology, biomedical imaging, geosciences, physics, and surveillance. Hyperspectral sensors look at objects using a vast portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Certain objects leave unique 'fingerprints' in the electromagnetic spectrum. Known as spectral signatures, these 'fingerprints' enable identification of the materials that make up a scanned object. For example, a spectral signature for oil helps geologists find new oil fields.

text:
Hyperspectral imaging captures and analyzes data across the electromagnetic spectrum to generate a spectrum for each pixel in a scene. The primary objective is to detect objects, identify materials, or reveal underlying processes by examining how different substances reflect or emit light. There are three main types of spectral imagers: push broom and whisk broom scanners, which scan a scene spatially over time; band sequential scanners, which collect images at successive wavelengths; and snapshot hyperspectral imagers, which use a staring array to record the full spectral data in a single exposure.

Unlike the human eye, which detects color through three broad bands—red, green, and blue—hyperspectral imaging divides the spectrum into many more, narrower bands. This method extends beyond visible light into near-infrared and shortwave infrared regions. The technique records continuous spectral bands with high wavelength resolution across a broad range of wavelengths. This differs from multiband imaging, which captures data at discrete, spaced intervals.

Engineers design hyperspectral sensors and their associated processing systems for use in astronomy, agriculture, molecular biology, biomedical imaging, geosciences, physics, and surveillance. These sensors analyze objects across a wide portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Materials exhibit unique responses to electromagnetic radiation, producing identifiable patterns known as spectral signatures. These signatures act like fingerprints, enabling precise material identification. For instance, a distinct spectral signature associated with oil allows geologists to locate potential oil reserves.

Hyperspectral imaging collects and processes data across the electromagnetic spectrum to capture the spectrum for each pixel in a scene. The goal is to identify materials, detect objects, or reveal processes by analyzing these spectral measurements. This method extends beyond visible light and allows for detailed analysis across a broad range of wavelengths. Hyperspectral imaging captures continuous spectral bands with fine wavelength resolution, distinguishing it from multiband imaging, which measures discrete, spaced bands.

Engineers design hyperspectral sensors and processing systems for use in astronomy, agriculture, molecular biology, biomedical imaging, geosciences, physics, and surveillance. These sensors analyze objects across a wide portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. Different materials reflect, absorb, and emit radiation in unique patterns, producing distinct spectral signatures—like fingerprints—that identify their composition. text:
In statistics, missing data, or missing values, occur when no data value is stored for the variable in an observation.  Missing data are a common occurrence and can have a significant effect on the conclusions that can be drawn from the data.
Missing data can occur because of nonresponse: no information is provided for one or more items or for a whole unit ("subject"). Some items are more likely to generate a nonresponse than others: for example items about private subjects such as income. Attrition is a type of missingness that can occur in longitudinal studies—for instance studying development where a measurement is repeated after a certain period of time. Missingness occurs when participants drop out before the test ends and one or more measurements are missing.
Data often are missing in research in economics, sociology, and political science because governments or private entities choose not to, or fail to, report critical statistics, or because the information is not available. Sometimes missing values are caused by the researcher—for example, when data collection is done improperly or mistakes are made in data entry.
These forms of missingness take different types, with different impacts on the validity of conclusions from research: Missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random.  Missing data can be handled similarly as censored data.

text: In statistical analysis, missing data—also referred to as missing values—arise when no value is recorded for a variable in a given observation. This phenomenon is widespread across research domains and can substantially influence the reliability and validity of analytical outcomes. Nonresponse is a frequent cause, occurring when participants fail to provide information for one or more items, or for an entire unit. Certain topics, particularly those involving personal or sensitive information such as income, are more prone to nonresponse due to privacy concerns. In longitudinal studies, where repeated measurements track change over time, attrition may lead to missing data when participants discontinue participation before the study concludes, resulting in incomplete records for one or more time points. The absence of data is especially common in fields like economics, sociology, and political science, where data may not be reported by governments or private organizations due to omission, failure to collect, or policy constraints. Additionally, researchers may inadvertently introduce missing values through errors in data collection or inaccurate data entry. Missing data are classified into three distinct mechanisms: missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random. Each mechanism carries different implications for statistical inference, as the pattern of absence can affect whether conclusions remain unbiased. Because of similarities in their treatment, missing data are often addressed using methods analogous to those used for censored data.

text:
In statistics, missing data—also referred to as missing values—arise when no value is recorded for a variable in a given observation. This phenomenon is widespread and can substantially influence the validity of analytical conclusions. Missingness may stem from nonresponse, where no information is provided for one or more variables, or for an entire unit, such as a person or household. Certain topics, particularly those involving personal or sensitive information like income, are more prone to nonresponse. In longitudinal studies—such as those tracking developmental changes over time—attrition contributes to missing data: participants may leave the study before follow-up measurements are completed, resulting in incomplete records.

Missing values are common in research across economics, sociology, and political science, often due to deliberate omissions or failures by governments or private organizations to report essential statistics. In some cases, missing data result from researcher error, including flawed data collection procedures or mistakes during data entry.

These patterns of missingness fall into three distinct categories, each with different implications for inference: missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR). The nature of the missingness affects how reliably conclusions can be drawn. While missing data differ in mechanism, they are sometimes addressed using methods similar to those used for censored data, particularly when the absence of a value carries meaningful information about the underlying process.

text:
In computing, a database is an organized collection of data stored and accessed electronically. Small databases can be stored on a file system, while large databases are hosted on computer clusters or cloud storage. The design of databases spans formal techniques and practical considerations, including data modeling, efficient data representation and storage, query languages, security and privacy of sensitive data, and distributed computing issues, including supporting concurrent access and fault tolerance.
A database management system (DBMS) is the software that interacts with end users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze the data. The DBMS software additionally encompasses the core facilities provided to administer the database. The sum total of the database, the DBMS and the associated applications can be referred to as a database system. Often the term "database" is also used loosely to refer to any of the DBMS, the database system or an application associated with the database.
Computer scientists may classify database management systems according to the database models that they support. Relational databases became dominant in the 1980s. These model data as rows and columns in a series of tables, and the vast majority use SQL for writing and querying data. In the 2000s, non-relational databases became popular, collectively referred to as NoSQL, because they use different query languages.

text:
A database is an organized collection of data stored and accessed electronically. Small databases may reside on a file system, while larger ones are typically deployed on computer clusters or cloud storage infrastructure. Database design integrates formal methods with practical requirements, addressing data modeling, efficient storage representation, query languages, protection of sensitive information, and distributed computing challenges such as concurrent access and fault tolerance.

The database management system (DBMS) is the software layer that facilitates interaction between end users, applications, and the database. It manages data capture and retrieval, provides core administrative functions, and ensures data integrity and access control. The complete system—encompassing the database, DBMS, and associated applications—is known as a database system. In common usage, the term "database" may refer to any of these components: the DBMS, the database system, or a supporting application.

DBMSs are categorized by the database models they support. Relational databases, which represent data as rows and columns within tables, gained dominance in the 1980s. They primarily use SQL for data manipulation and querying. In the 2000s, non-relational databases emerged as a significant alternative, collectively termed NoSQL, due to their use of different query languages and data models.

text: Dynamic programming emerged in the 1950s as a method devised by Richard Bellman to handle complex decision processes. It applies to problems where choices made at one point affect what’s possible later—common in aerospace engineering, economics, and planning. The core idea is breaking a large problem into smaller ones that share components. If solving these smaller parts correctly leads to a solution for the whole, the problem has optimal substructure. That condition allows building up a solution recursively: the best choice now depends on the best outcomes achievable from future states. This link between current decisions and future outcomes is captured in the Bellman equation, a formal expression of how value at one stage relates to values at others. Not every problem fits this pattern. But for those that do, the structure enables efficient computation by avoiding redundant calculations—each sub-problem is solved once and stored. The technique isn’t a shortcut; it’s a way to exploit order and repetition in problems that evolve over time. Its power lies in this precision: not every system allows it, but when it applies, the result is a clear path from input to solution.

text:
Blood cultures are still considered the definitive test for confirming bacteremia versus systemic inflammation without infection. Clinically, negative results over 48 to 72 hours typically rule out bacteremia. But modern blood culture systems now detect growth much faster, undermining that time-based threshold. This study assessed how quickly bacteremia is detected, the likelihood of a positive result after 24 hours, and which patient factors delay detection.

Researchers reviewed records from 801 adult patients with monomicrobial bacteremia over three years at a university-affiliated hospital. Data were pulled directly from electronic health records. Univariate and multivariate models identified factors linked to longer time-to-positivity (TTP), and the residual risk of bacteremia was estimated when cultures stayed negative at 24 hours.

The average age was 65 (IQR 54–73), and 534 patients were male. Median TTP was 15.7 hours (IQR 13.5–19.3), and 85.3% of episodes had TTP within 24 hours. Antibiotics given before culture collection were independently linked to longer TTP (adjusted OR 1.77; 95% CI 1.14–2.74, p<0.01). If cultures remained negative after 24 hours, the chance of actual bacteremia was 1.8% (95% CI 1.46–2.14).

In settings with timely lab processing, a negative result at 24 hours strongly suggests absence of bacteremia. This can help shift focus in diagnosis and guide decisions on continuing or stopping antibiotics. The approach may support antimicrobial stewardship, but its real-world effectiveness needs testing in prospective studies.

text: In statistical analysis, missing data—values not recorded for a variable in a specific observation—occur frequently across research fields and compromise the reliability of results. Nonresponse is a common source, happening when individuals skip questions or fail to complete surveys entirely. Sensitive topics like income often see higher nonresponse rates, driven by concerns over privacy. In longitudinal studies, where data are collected repeatedly over time, participants who drop out before the study ends leave gaps in records, especially at later time points. This kind of missingness is common in economics, sociology, and political science, where governments or private entities may not report data due to oversight, lack of collection, or policy restrictions. Some missing data arise from human error—incorrect data entry or flawed collection procedures. These omissions fall into three categories: missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random. The mechanism behind the absence shapes how much conclusions might be biased. Because missing data and censored data share structural similarities in how they affect inference, statistical approaches for handling one often apply to the other.

Nigeria’s economy, still evolving but deeply disrupted by armed conflict, grapples with entrenched poverty and alarmingly high rates of child illness. Among the most pressing concerns is the health of young children, which remains closely tied to the education level of their mothers—a key factor in how families navigate hardship. The connection between maternal schooling and child well-being is not linear, nor is it equally powerful across all households. What remains unclear is whether a specific number of years in school triggers a measurable decline in severe undernutrition, especially in areas where violence persists.

This analysis draws on two national surveys—2008 and 2013 Nigerian Demographic and Health Surveys—tracking 25,917 children and their mothers. To account for variation in how maternal education influences outcomes depending on household conditions, the researchers applied Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) to calculate Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATEs). The results show that going beyond the nine-year compulsory education baseline offers measurable benefits. When a mother completes ten or more years of schooling, her child’s risk of severe undernutrition drops, even amid active conflict. This suggests that education, once extended past a minimum threshold, acts as a meaningful buffer against health deterioration in fragile environments. The findings point to a practical rationale for integrating maternal education into public health strategies in war-affected regions.

text: Under Cairo’s relentless sun, a young man walks a cracked sidewalk where heat shimmers off the pavement. He reaches the edge of Tahrir Square, its edges blurred by heat haze. At the entrance, a woman stands, not looking at him, but her posture holds his attention—still, observant. He doesn’t approach. Instead, images form behind his eyes: a man who talks too much, another who speaks in half-truths, a third who moves like someone carrying something heavy. These aren’t roles he chooses. They’re voices that rise in his mind, each version testing a different way to speak, to stand, to be seen. He sees them arguing quietly, not with words, but with the shape of their bodies, the tilt of a shoulder, the pause before a sentence. The woman in his mind shifts too—not her face, but her presence, as if she’s listening to all of them at once. None of this lasts. The heat presses down. He blinks. The square is empty again. No one has moved. No one has spoken. He stands where he is, not waiting, not deciding, just listening to the silence that follows the kind of thoughts that don’t leave after they begin.

text:
Hyperspectral imaging records the electromagnetic response of every pixel in a scene, building a detailed spectrum for each point. Instead of relying on broad color channels like the human eye’s red, green, and blue receptors, it splits the spectrum into dozens or hundreds of narrow, contiguous bands. This includes not only visible light but extends into near-infrared and shortwave infrared regions, capturing subtle variations in how materials reflect or emit energy.

The technology operates through several methods. Push broom and whisk broom scanners move across a scene over time, scanning spatially while collecting spectral data. Band sequential imagers acquire images at successive wavelengths, building up the full spectrum in sequence. Snapshot hyperspectral imagers, in contrast, use a staring array to capture the complete spectral data in one exposure, without motion.

These systems are built for demanding fields: astronomy, agriculture, molecular biology, biomedical imaging, geosciences, physics, and surveillance. The core principle lies in how materials interact with electromagnetic radiation—each substance produces a unique pattern of reflection and emission. These patterns, called spectral signatures, serve as identifiers, much like fingerprints. When a known signature for oil appears in a rock formation, for example, it signals possible reserves. Unlike multiband imaging, which samples at fixed, spaced intervals, hyperspectral systems collect continuous data across a broad wavelength range with high resolution. This allows for more precise material differentiation, critical in detecting subtle changes or hidden features in complex environments.

text: Herman Hollerith created the tabulating machine, an electromechanical device, to process data from punched cards. It debuted during the 1890 U.S. Census, where it dramatically reduced the time needed to tabulate results. Later models were adopted in business for tasks like accounting and tracking inventory. The machine’s success contributed to the development of unit record systems and laid the foundation for the data processing industry. In 1931, the New York World described a large, custom-built tabulator built by IBM for Columbia University as "super computing," one of the earliest recorded uses of that term.

text:
A two-step trial evaluated the cost-effectiveness of endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) for mediastinal staging in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients in France. First, standardized EBUS-TBNA training was implemented at designated hospitals. Then, a multicenter, prospective study enrolled individuals with suspected NSCLC and at least one mediastinal lymph node measuring over 1 cm in diameter. EBUS-TBNA was performed as the initial staging procedure; when results were negative or uncertain, patients underwent mediastinoscopy or surgery, guided by PET scan outcomes. All procedure-related costs tied to lymph node status assessment were documented.

Of the 163 patients included, EBUS-TBNA delivered a conclusive result in 149 (91%), with a node positivity rate of 52%. The test showed strong diagnostic performance, with positive predictive value at 100% and negative predictive value at 90%. The procedure prevented the need for mediastinoscopy in 80% of cases. Economic analysis revealed EBUS-TBNA generated an average cost saving of €1,450 per patient. Even under challenging assumptions—such as using general anesthesia or a 30% increase in procedure cost—savings remained significant, at €994 and €1,427 per patient, respectively. The results confirm that EBUS-TBNA is a cost-effective approach for NSCLC staging, provided training standards and center certification are met.

text:
A database is an electronic collection of data structured for efficient storage and retrieval. Some small databases exist as files on local systems, but most large-scale deployments run on clusters or cloud infrastructure. Designing a database involves modeling data, choosing storage formats, building query languages, securing sensitive content, and solving problems like simultaneous access and system failures.

The database management system (DBMS) is the software that sits between users, applications, and the stored data. It handles how data is entered and fetched, manages backups and user permissions, and enforces consistency across changes. The full setup—database, DBMS, and supporting apps—forms a database system. In everyday language, "database" often refers to any part of this stack: the DBMS itself, the entire system, or a tool that uses it.

DBMSs are grouped by the data models they rely on. Relational databases, which organize information into tables of rows and columns, became standard in the 1980s. They use SQL for querying and updating data. Starting in the 2000s, a different approach gained traction: non-relational systems, collectively known as NoSQL. These differ in how they store data and often use query languages that aren’t based on SQL.

An explosion occurred at the EQ Resource Recovery chemical plant in Romulus, a suburb southeast of Detroit, prompting voluntary evacuations for residents within a half-mile radius on Tuesday. Following the explosion, multiple Michigan-based law firms initiated class action lawsuits on behalf of affected residents, with additional legal actions under consideration. In 2000, at age 36, Thin was previously imprisoned after being taken from a Suu Kyi rally by special police. She was held at Insein prison as part of a wider crackdown on opposition figures.

text:
Blood cultures remain the gold standard for confirming bacteremia versus systemic inflammation without infection. Clinically, negative results over 48 to 72 hours typically exclude bacteremia. However, modern blood culture systems detect growth more rapidly, challenging this time-based threshold. This study examined detection speed, the likelihood of positive results after 24 hours, and patient factors delaying detection.

Researchers analyzed records from 801 adult patients with monomicrobial bacteremia over three years at a university-affiliated hospital. Data were sourced directly from electronic health records. Univariate and multivariate models identified factors associated with longer time-to-positivity (TTP), and the residual risk of bacteremia was estimated when cultures remained negative at 24 hours.

Patients had an average age of 65 (IQR 54–73), with 534 being male. Median TTP was 15.7 hours (IQR 13.5–19.3), and 85.3% of episodes had TTP within 24 hours. Antibiotics administered before culture collection were independently linked to longer TTP (adjusted OR 1.77; 95% CI 1.14–2.74, p<0.01). If cultures were negative after 24 hours, the probability of actual bacteremia was 1.8% (95% CI 1.46–2.14).

In settings with timely lab processing, a negative result at 24 hours strongly suggests the absence of bacteremia. This finding can aid diagnosis and guide decisions on continuing or stopping antibiotics. The approach may support antimicrobial stewardship, but its real-world effectiveness requires validation in prospective studies.

Dean is dead. The Dead Man remains undisturbed. Garrett stands alone, accompanied only by the Goddamn Parrot, its cries piercing the silence. Restlessness gnaws at him. Then Winger appears, unnamed but pressing, with information about a woman called Maggie Jenn. Garrett accepts the case.

Maggie Jenn isn't the client Garrett expected. She hired him to find her daughter, Emerald. Initially, the investigation shows promise—clues, locations, a glimmer of hope. Then, violence erupts. A strike to the neck. Darkness. Garrett regains consciousness in the Bledsoe sanatorium, strapped to a chair, the air heavy with antiseptic and deceit.

Upon escape, the truth becomes clear: Grange Cleaver, known as The Rainmaker, orchestrated the kidnapping and ambush. But this was part of something older, more sinister. Morley joins Garrett, driven by instinct rather than evidence. They pursue Cleaver through the city's underbelly, but he slips away like mist. Morley doesn't return.

Maggie's story unravels. Rumors spread—she may not be a grieving mother but something more sinister, perhaps the storm itself. The Outfit closes in, and the City Watch stumbles into the chaos. All vie for control of the brewing tempest.

Then Cleaver is found dead in a basement, throat torn out. There are no witnesses, no confession. The city relaxes, but Garrett doesn't. He knows the storm hasn't ended; it has merely changed course. Someone else lurks in the shadows, watching.

Detective Inspector John Rebus, aware of Jack's struggles with addiction and stress, interviews Andrew MacMillan, a former ally of Jack's now in custody for murdering his wife. Evidence accumulates gradually: discrepancies in alibis, an encrypted message in Jack's office, and a hotel receipt under a false name. Rebus is unconvinced of Jack's guilt, suspecting instead that someone exploited Jack's personal struggles to destroy him completely.

text: In Queensland's wet tropical rainforests, large trees—defined as those with a diameter at breast height (DBH) of 10 cm or more—significantly influence the forest's structure and function. In a study across 20 plots, each spanning 0.5 hectares, trees with a DBH of 70 cm or more comprised just 2.4% of all stems but contributed approximately one-third of the total above-ground biomass. The variability in biomass between these plots strongly correlates with the number and spatial arrangement of these largest trees. Notably, the top 5% of trees by size possessed enough mass to predict total plot biomass with around 85% accuracy. Unlike rainforests in Africa and the Americas, where a few dominant species drive biomass accumulation, Australian forests distribute large-tree potential more broadly across species. About ten percent of species account for half the biomass, indicating a less extreme hyperdominance. This pattern arises from a dense mix of large trees and moderately sized ones, which together enhance the system's resilience against disturbances and climate-induced shifts. The coexistence of high biomass, diverse species, and abundant large trees suggests this ecosystem may retain significant carbon stores over time, even under changing conditions.

text: One afternoon, the narrator of *Kangaroo Notebook* experienced an odd prickling sensation on his leg, noticeable but indistinguishable. By morning, small pale bumps had appeared on his shins. He visited a clinic, spoke with the doctor, and after an hour-long wait, was referred to the city hospital. There, a thin man in a starched coat instructed him to bathe in Hell Valley's hot springs. The narrator was then connected to a catheter and IV, wheeled on a metal bed through an underground tunnel. The descent was slow, the air dense with steam. Below, the environment was not empty but convoluted. Ferrymen's shouts mixed with faint, submerged voices, children's silhouettes wandered through fog, and nurses with pale lips and long fingers lingered near doorways. A chiropractor who taught karate and knew lethal techniques offered him a drink. The narrator inquired about the purpose, but received no answer. He wandered this place, seeking to understand his situation, but encountered only echoes.

text: Herman Hollerith invented the tabulating machine, an electromechanical device that processed data from punched cards. It first appeared during the 1890 U.S. Census, significantly cutting the time required to tabulate results. Businesses later adopted improved models for tasks like accounting and inventory tracking. This machine's success led to the creation of unit record systems, forming the basis for the data processing industry. Notably, the New York World referred to a large IBM-built tabulator for Columbia University in 1931 as "super computing," marking one of the earliest uses of that term.

text: Jean Baudrillard argued that the Gulf War was not a genuine conflict but rather a staged atrocity presented as such. The media's portrayal, carefully curated to fit a specific narrative, blurred the line between real combat and its constructed representation. As a result, the public remained uncertain about the authenticity of what they witnessed, unable to discern the extent to which events had been manipulated for effect.

text:
Hyperspectral imaging captures the electromagnetic response of each pixel in a scene, creating a detailed spectrum for every point. It differs from the human eye's broad color channels by dividing the spectrum into numerous narrow, adjacent bands, encompassing visible light, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared regions. This reveals subtle material reflections or emissions.

The technology employs various methods. Push broom and whisk broom scanners move across a scene, collecting spatial and spectral data over time. Band sequential imagers acquire images at successive wavelengths, building the full spectrum sequentially. Snapshot hyperspectral imagers use a staring array to capture complete spectral data in a single exposure, without movement.

These systems serve specialized applications: astronomy, agriculture, molecular biology, biomedical imaging, geosciences, physics, and surveillance. The key lies in material interactions with electromagnetic radiation. Each substance produces a unique reflection and emission pattern called a spectral signature, acting as an identifier. For instance, detecting an oil signature in rock formations may indicate potential reserves. Unlike multiband imaging with fixed intervals, hyperspectral systems gather continuous, high-resolution data across a broad wavelength range. This enables precise material differentiation, crucial for detecting subtle changes or hidden features in complex environments.

text:
A database stores data in a structured format, enabling efficient retrieval and management. Small databases may reside on local systems, while larger ones typically operate on clusters or cloud platforms. Designing a database requires modeling data, selecting storage formats, developing query languages, protecting sensitive information, and addressing issues like concurrent access and system failures.

The database management system (DBMS) acts as an intermediary between users, applications, and the stored data. It oversees data input and retrieval, manages backups and user permissions, and ensures consistency across modifications. Together, the database, DBMS, and supporting applications constitute a database system. Commonly, the term "database" may refer to any of these components: the DBMS, the entire system, or the tools that utilize it.

DBMSs are categorized based on the data models they employ. Relational databases, which organize data into tables comprising rows and columns, became prevalent in the 1980s. These systems utilize SQL for data queries and updates. Beginning in the 2000s, non-relational databases, collectively termed NoSQL, gained popularity. These systems vary in their data storage methods and often employ query languages distinct from SQL.

A database is an electronic collection of data structured for efficient storage and retrieval. Some small databases exist as files on local systems, but most large-scale deployments run on clusters or cloud infrastructure. Designing a database involves modeling data, choosing storage formats, building query languages, securing sensitive content, and solving problems like simultaneous access and system failures.

The database management system (DBMS) is the software that sits between users, applications, and the stored data. It handles how data is entered and fetched, manages backups and user permissions, and enforces consistency across changes. The full setup—database, DBMS, and supporting apps—forms a database system. In everyday language, "database" often refers to any part of this stack: the DBMS itself, the entire system, or a tool that uses it.

DBMSs are grouped by the data models they rely on. Relational databases, which organize information into tables of rows and columns, became standard in the 1980s. They use SQL for querying and updating data. Starting in the 2000s, a different approach gained traction: non-relational systems, collectively known as NoSQL. These differ in how they store data and often use query languages that aren’t based on SQL.

text:
A two-step trial assessed the cost-effectiveness of endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) for mediastinal staging in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients across France. The first phase involved implementing standardized EBUS-TBNA training at selected hospitals. In the second phase, a multicenter, prospective study enrolled patients with suspected NSCLC and at least one mediastinal lymph node larger than 1 cm. EBUS-TBNA served as the initial staging procedure; when results were inconclusive, patients underwent mediastinoscopy or surgery based on PET scan findings. All costs associated with these procedures were recorded.

Out of 163 patients, EBUS-TBNA provided definitive results for 149 (91%), with a 52% node positivity rate. The test demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, with a positive predictive value of 100% and a negative predictive value of 90%. The procedure eliminated the need for mediastinoscopy in 80% of cases. Economic analysis showed that EBUS-TBNA saved an average of €1,450 per patient. Even under conservative assumptions, such as using general anesthesia or a 30% increase in procedure cost, the savings remained substantial at €994 and €1,427 per patient, respectively. These findings confirm that EBUS-TBNA is a cost-effective method for NSCLC staging, provided training and center certification standards are maintained.
